newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open higher before employment data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open higher before employment data.

text.p: U.S. government securities prices opened narrowly higher on Thursday as investors awaited the simultaneous releases of weekly jobless claims data and the June payroll employment report.

The Labor Department's jobless claims data for the latest week are expected to show that 336,000 new claims for state unemployment insurance were filed in the week ended June 28, according to economists polled by Reuters.
The June monthly payroll employment report is also due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.

Monthly payroll employment reports are almost always released on a Friday. This report is being released on Thursday, however, because government offices and financial markets will be closed on Friday due to the Fourth of July Independence Day holiday.
Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that payrolls grew by 222,000 jobs in June after fairly slight growth of 138,000 new jobs in May.
Analysts said payroll growth of fewer than 200,000 new jobs for June would be constructive for the bond market while payroll growth that exceeded 250,000 jobs could hurt it.

The market will also look at the Labor Department's release of the unemployment rate, expected to be 4.8 percent, unchanged from May. Hourly earnings are forecast to be up 0.4 percent in June after a 0.3 percent rise in May. The length of the average workweek is expected to rise to 34.6 hours in June from 34.5 hours in May.
Analysts said the market was enjoying a good tone before the release of the data, following the Federal Reserve's decision at its July 1-2 policy meeting to leave interest rates unchanged.
Most European bond markets were also slightly higher overnight, they said.
In initial dealings, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was priced at 99 even, up 3/32 to yield 6.70 percent.
Ten-year notes were unchanged at 101-18/32, with a yield of 6.41 percent. The five-year note was up 1/32 at 99-26/32 yielding 6.29 percent.
Three-month bill rates were down one basis point to 5.08 percent. Six-month and year bill rates were each up one basis point to 5.11 percent and 5.34 percent, respectively.
Two-year notes were unchanged, yielding 6.02 percent.
